narrative: The model estimated a 16% chance that you will fail your final year. Under the school’s decision rule, that risk is enough to require remedial courses, though it is a risk flag rather than a certainty. The three most influential factors were your past class failures, your intention to continue to higher education, and the quality of your family relationships. Importantly, all three pushed your risk downward, toward passing. You have no recorded past failures, which matches the average among students who passed; you want to continue to higher education, as did every passing student in the comparison group; and your family relationships are good, which was also common among passers. So the requirement is not explained by a history of failure or lack of ambition. The overall flag instead reflects the balance of your day-to-day profile, especially two practical concerns: you study less than two hours a week, while most passing students study two to five hours, and you have nine absences, well above the passing average of about four. To improve, treat the remedial courses as a chance to build a steadier weekly study routine, attend every class, and use your good family support to stay accountable. Keep your higher-education goal visible and ask for help early when a subject starts to slip.
